title: First Bad Version
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential version checking versus binary search on the monotonic good-then-bad boundary.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: You are given n versions [1, 2, ..., n], and you want to find the first bad one, given that once a version is bad, all versions after it are bad too. You are given an API isBadVersion(version) that returns whether a given version is bad. Find the first bad version using as few calls to this API as possible.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n (total versions), an isBadVersion(v) API"],["Output","The first (smallest) bad version"],["Goal","Minimize calls to isBadVersion, ideally O(log n)"],["Constraints","1 <= bad <= n <= 2^31 - 1"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Once true, always true afterward\" (a monotonic boolean condition)","Binary search on the answer: find the exact boundary where the condition flips"],["\"Minimize calls to an expensive check function\"","Binary search minimizes the number of isBadVersion calls to O(log n)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Versions form a sequence where everything before the first bad version is good, and everything from the first bad version onward is bad. This "good...good, bad...bad" monotonic shape is exactly the structure binary search exploits to find the exact transition point.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Where a Product Recall Batch Begins
blocks.text: Picture a production line's output numbered sequentially, where a defect started at some unknown point and every unit after it is also defective. Testing a middle unit tells you whether the defect started before or at-or-after that point, letting you narrow down the exact starting unit quickly.

blocks.caption: Good versions then bad versions is a monotonic boolean sequence, letting binary search find the exact boundary

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 5, first bad version = 4
Result: 4. Versions 1-3 are good, versions 4-5 are bad; the first bad one is 4.
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every version sequentially from 1 upward, notice that isBadVersion forms a monotonic "false, false, ..., true, true, ..." sequence, and binary search can directly locate the exact index where it flips from false to true.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If isBadVersion(mid) is true, the first bad version is at mid or somewhere before it, so the search range's upper bound can move to mid.

Observation 2: If isBadVersion(mid) is false, the first bad version must be strictly after mid, so the lower bound can move to mid+1.

Observation 3: This is the standard "find the first true in a monotonic false-then-true sequence" binary search template, converging when lo equals hi.

Observation 4: Minimizing calls to isBadVersion (an expensive API call, conceptually) is exactly what binary search achieves, reducing calls from O(n) to O(log n).
This leads to binary searching directly on the version number: if isBadVersion(mid) is true, search the left half (including mid); otherwise, search the right half (excluding mid).
6. Brute Force Solution
Check versions 1, 2, 3, ... in order, calling isBadVersion on each, stopping at the first one that is bad.
Step by step algorithm

items: Starting from version 1, call isBadVersion(v) for each v in increasing order.
Return the first v for which isBadVersion(v) is true.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking versions sequentially directly finds the first bad one, guaranteed correct.
This could call isBadVersion up to n times, far more than necessary given the monotonic structure.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) calls to isBadVersion in the worst case.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: the monotonic good-then-bad structure allows binary search to find the exact boundary in O(log n) calls instead of O(n).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sequential checking is unnecessary: the monotonic nature of isBadVersion (once true, always true afterward) means a single check at any midpoint tells you definitively which half contains the boundary.

How the search proceeds: if isBadVersion(mid) is true, the answer is mid or earlier, so move hi to mid; if false, the answer is strictly later, so move lo to mid+1.

Convergence: since the range strictly shrinks each step, lo and hi converge to the exact first bad version.

The core idea: binary search directly on the version number, using isBadVersion as the monotonic condition.
Binary search with lo=1, hi=n. At each step, check isBadVersion(mid); move hi to mid if bad, or lo to mid+1 if not. Stop when lo equals hi.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for n = 5, first bad version = 4

blocks.caption: Binary search on the monotonic boolean condition converges on the exact boundary

blocks.text: Why This Works

Because the sequence of versions is monotonic (all good versions come before all bad versions), the binary search invariant "the first bad version lies within [lo, hi]" is preserved at every step: moving hi to mid when isBadVersion(mid) is true never excludes a smaller valid answer (since mid itself is a valid candidate), and moving lo to mid+1 when false correctly excludes mid (known good). This converges exactly on the first bad version.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) calls to isBadVersion.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
First Bad Version is the canonical "binary search on a monotonic boolean condition" problem, minimizing calls to an expensive check function by finding the exact true/false boundary directly.
Common Mistakes

items: Using hi = mid - 1 instead of hi = mid when the version is bad, which could skip over the actual first bad version.
Not minimizing API calls at all by checking versions sequentially, missing the point of the problem.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly naming this as "binary search on the answer, using a monotonic predicate" ties it to a widely reusable technique beyond just this specific problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimize calls to an expensive check with a monotonic true/false result", think: binary search directly on the boundary.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you handle this if isBadVersion had a rate limit or cost per call?
How would you find the LAST good version instead, using the same technique?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "binary search on the answer" problem where a monotonic condition replaces a direct value comparison.
Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days, Koko Eating Bananas, and similar problems using the identical monotonic-boundary binary search template.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sequential checking costs O(n) API calls; binary search costs O(log n), the expected and required solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: binary search on a monotonic boolean condition, finding the exact false-to-true boundary.
Core Idea: if isBadVersion(mid) is true, search left (inclusive of mid); otherwise search strictly right.
Time: O(n) for sequential checking, O(log n) for binary search.
Most Important Observation: a monotonic true/false sequence is just as valid a binary-search target as a sorted array of values.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, widely applicable binary-search-on-a-predicate problem.
One line memory trick: bad means search left (inclusive), good means search right (exclusive).
